articles.title: “Borderline” is likely an “identity” or “emotional” disorder, but definitely not a “personality” disorder: A commentary on Sharp et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Orestis Zavlis
articles.abstract: In a 17-year longitudinal study, Sharp et al. (2026) report that “self-functioning” outperforms “interpersonal functioning” in predicting later borderline pathology, concluding that the core and distinguishing features of “personality disorder” lie in the “representation of self”. In this commentary, I suggest that these findings can be interpreted in at least two alternative ways. First, I argue that when we take the authors’ findings at face value, we reach the conclusion that (borderline) personality disorder can be understood as an “identity disorder” given that its main impairments lie in “the representation of self”. Second, I argue that when examined closely, the authors’ findings suggest that “(borderline) personality disorder” is an “emotional disorder”, given that the predictor of “self-functioning” is constructed with items that encode emotional, not self-related, pathology. Finally, I conclude by noting that whichever way Sharp et al.’s findings are interpreted, they cannot support the inference that “(borderline) personality disorder” is in any way about “personality”.

articles.title: Suicide imagery subtypes and their relationships with suicide behaviour: a mixed-methods evaluation
articles.authors: Ann Martin; Cassandra Chakouch; Demee Rheinberger; Peter McEvoy; Julie Lin Ji; Fiona Shand
articles.abstract:
Objective: Mental imagery about suicide is a commonly experienced risk factor for suicide, but subtypes and their relationships to behaviour remain largely unexplored. This study aims to identify and describe common themes in suicide imagery content, perceived function, and subjective meaning in relation to suicide behaviour. 
Method: Participants (N=20) provided quantitative and qualitative data about content, perceived function, and subjective meaning across 30 unique instances of suicide imagery via online surveys and semi-structured interviews. 
Results: Framework Analysis resulted in five key themes: (a) Determination imagery depicting a single action script detailing a chosen suicide method, (b) Solution imagery highlighting wanted impacts of suicide, (c) Mental Exercise or fantasy imagery, (d) Discouraging imagery of unwanted impacts of suicide, and (e) Consideration imagery weighing up different methods. Determination and Solution imagery were commonly associated with suicide behaviour. Imagery prior to attempt was often deliberately constructed, wanted, and prolonged (Median duration = 90 minutes).
Conclusions: Findings suggest that imagery themes may vary on dimensions reflecting facilitation and deterrence of behaviour, which may interact to produce ambivalence. In addition to volitional impacts via suicide action script rehearsal, suicide imagery may increase motivation towards suicide. Prior to attempt, suicide imagery may be acceptable, comforting, or even sought after. This study provides a nuanced understanding of suicide imagery subtypes in relation to suicide behaviour and provides a framework to assist clinicians in assessment and formulation.

articles.title: Eliciting Spontaneous Belief-Congruent Action Anticipation in Adults Using Structured Familiarization in Rich Nonverbal Narratives
articles.authors: Fumihiro Kano; Josep Call; Nicolas Goppold; Kazuhide Hashiya; Mitsuhiko Ishikawa; Xianwei Meng; Emilie Rapport Munro; Hiroshi Nitta; Yuki Ogawa; Atsushi Senju
articles.abstract: Humans and other animals predict others’ actions from mental states, even when those states misrepresent reality. The anticipatory-looking false-belief (ALFB) task assesses belief-congruent action prediction without verbal responses, yet its reliability remains debated. Across six experiments, we tested 302 adults using false-belief events embedded in rich nonverbal narratives. We progressively refined familiarization while keeping the critical false-belief induction and test events unchanged. Reliable belief-congruent anticipatory looking emerged after familiarization was restructured, possibly because this reduced reliance on spatial heuristics and encouraged perspective taking. Explicit verbal prediction questions strengthened performance but were unnecessary. The refined procedure was confirmed within the original laboratory and independently replicated in a second laboratory. These findings indicate that belief-congruent action prediction is sensitive to task procedures, especially the predictive structure of familiarization. Our study provides a foundation for evaluating spontaneous theory of mind across development and species.

articles.title: A set of dynamical rules for conversational progression act as a precursor to collective cognition
articles.authors: Zachary P Rosen
articles.abstract: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. This report provides a functional description of how conversation states are updated in terms of information-theoretic processes, while analyzing a corpus of 5,447 conversations in nine typologically diverse languages. Our results show that individuals form a strongly connected distributed computational system during conversation, which generates new information according to a power-law distribution. This enables speakers to encode and solve a potentially unbounded number of problems and ideas, simply by conversing.

articles.title: Do young children represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities?
articles.authors: Urvi Maheshwari; Caren Walker; David Barner
articles.abstract: A prominent hypothesis in the literature on logical reasoning suggests that, unlike human adults and older children, 3-year-olds deploy a “minimal representation of possibility” when reasoning about the existence of a reward in one of two possible locations. On this view, children are unable to represent two mutually exclusive possibilities simultaneously, and instead commit to one location for the reward in a pair of possible locations, only considering the second location once they have evidence that their first choice is not correct. Although this hypothesis may explain children’s struggles on various tests of modal reasoning, the idea that children may represent possible reward locations sequentially (rather than simultaneously) has not been directly tested. In two studies, we asked 24- to 38-month-olds to choose two of three reward locations, one of which was physically impossible. We found that children aged 31 to 38 months selected the two possible locations without feedback when required to make a simultaneous choice. We argue that these data are compatible with an ability to represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities.

articles.title: A Taxonomy of Misleading Mental Health Content Online
articles.authors: Nicole Bizzotto
articles.abstract: Online mental health communication can mislead without containing demonstrably incorrect claims. This article introduces a taxonomy of misleading online mental health content, distinguishing between source-, message-, and decoding-level misleadingness. It provides researchers, clinicians, and online platforms with a framework for identifying potentially harmful mental health content online that veracity-based approaches may overlook.

articles.title: Underestimating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences: an audit of six surprising SCORE replication failures.
articles.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles.abstract: The Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) project recently published a large-scale replication project within the social and behavioural sciences. The authors replicated only 151 of 274 (55%) claims, a finding covered by major outlets such as the New York Times and Forbes. Here, I audited SCORE replications of six studies where at least one claim surprisingly failed to replicate. These failures were surprising because the original study produced a p < .01 while the replication yielded a significant effect in the opposite direction. I show that, of the 12 claims tested across these six replications, five were miscategorised as failed replications because of data analysis and interpretation problems, and six replications were invalid because of poor data quality and an error in the replication’s experiment code. I conclude that individual replications within replicability projects may benefit from more thorough peer review, and that a more comprehensive audit is necessary before we can be confident in the project’s overall replicability estimate.

articles.title: The social ecology of development: The changing structure of preschoolers’ everyday experiences at home
articles.authors: Nele-Pauline Suffo; Anas Suffo; Pierre-Etienne Martin; Yujin Kim; Anam Zahra; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles.abstract: Everyday social interactions shape human psychological development. Research, however, has primarily relied on controlled settings or brief observations; consequently, the nature of naturalistic everyday experiences remains largely unstudied. To address this gap, we developed an automated multimodal processing pipeline to analyze a large egocentric corpus of naturalistic everyday experiences from 107 children aged three to five years in Germany (267.52 hours). The pipeline detects faces, persons, proximity, and speech types to classify time into interacting, available, or alone states. Results indicate a significant ecological reorganization: social interaction dominates at age three and declines towards a more even distribution between states at age six. Conversational agency remains stable throughout preschool, with children sharing it nearly equally with conversational partners. Crucially, social interactions change in their structure in that isolated social cues become significantly less predictive of interactions with age. Thus, preschool social interactions become less frequent but more diverse with development.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects like Wikipedia rely on sequential collaboration, where individual contributors iteratively revise a shared product. While previous research has examined wikis for collaborative writing and sequential collaboration for numerical judgments, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on collaborative writing, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested whether higher variation in contributors’ expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared text. In an experiment with 413 participants, we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation resulted in more information being incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the speed of information accumulation, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors’ knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: Differential effects of individual versus consensus evaluations of narrator-to-story fit on the experience and outcomes of narrative listening.
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Khadija Faiz; Amy Francis; Elizabeth Leivers; Laurie Sin; Hannah Jones; Nadine Lavan; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: While a reader might imagine the narrator's and characters' voices in a written book, a spoken narrative solidifies the relationship between the narrator and the text. Here, we report two experiments investigating how perceived narrator-to-story fit affects narrative listening enjoyment and other listening outcomes. In a first experiment (N=400 participants), we manipulated the gender-related congruence between the expected and heard narrator of four spoken narratives in a willingness-to-wait paradigm. We found that listeners were more likely to continue listening to congruent than incongruent stories, but did not enjoy them more or comprehend them more accurately. However, we observed a dissociation in the observed effects of perceived narrator-to-story fit: specifically, higher individual evaluations significantly increased enjoyment, while both higher individual and (aggregated) mean fit ratings predicted greater motivation to continue listening. This suggested that crowd-sourced data may be less effective than personal taste when predicting narrative listening enjoyment. Indeed, a second experiment using a larger number of stories showed that participants’ enjoyment of spoken narratives is most strongly predicted by within-sample individual fit ratings, but not by within- or between-group aggregate ratings. Our findings provide evidence to support personalisation of narration as a way to promote enjoyment of spoken narratives and, potentially, audiobooks.

articles.title: Imagining, fast and slow: Dissociating reference-frame speed and content speed in mental simulation
articles.authors: Hanbei Zhou; Ash Bu; Tomer David Ullman
articles.abstract: Research on the imagination has examined how changing the contents and spatial framing of a mental scenes changes that scene. But hardly any work has changing the \textit{temporal} reference frame of the imagination. For an ideal simulator, changing the frame-rate in which something is imagined should not matter for scene content, but it is unknown whether changing the temporal frame affects people's imagination. Across three studies and six experiments (N = 223 after exclusions), participants watched stylized and naturalistic scenarios  of projectile and pendulum motion at different playback speeds, and continued them in their mind. Our set-up dissociates temporal reference frame from content speed, which allowed us to compare people's predictions to simulation models that do or don't separate content from temporal frame. We found that participants could adjust their imagined temporal reference. Participants also kept content separate from reference-frame speed in realistic (but not stylized) scenes.

articles.title: Prior information about another’s emotional state shapes the perceptual representation of their facial expressions
articles.authors: Igne Jasukaityte; Margaret Cecilia Jackson; Patric Bach
articles.abstract: Context is known to change how people evaluate facial expressions. However, predictive processing  accounts  claim  that  context  should  also  shape faceperceptual  representation, causing objectively identical expressions to appear different perceptually. We tested thisin five experiments with English-speaking adults in the UK and Ireland,recruited through a university participant pool and online platforms (total N= 413; 18–49 years; data collected 2023–2026).Participants heard how a person was feeling, watched that person’s ambiguous expression change towards a congruent or incongruent emotion, and judged the expression’s final seen emotional state. Expressions were rated as happier after happystatementsand sadder after sad statements (Experiment 1a), replicating prior work. However, they were also rated as more intense when congruent with prior statements than when incongruent (Experiment 1b), ruling out biases from statement-to-response mappings. When participants perceptually compared final  expressions  with  slightly  more  or  less  expressive  probe  faces,  they  generally overestimated faceexpressiveness (Experiments 2a, 2b). Crucially, this overestimation was larger for expressionscongruent with prior expectations, but only when the probe appeared after a longer delay (1000 vs 333 ms). The same pattern emerged when the emotion was not explicitly stated but inferred from a variety of news that participants delivered to the person (Experiment 3). Prior knowledge of another’s emotional state therefore shapes notonlythe evaluation of the person’s facial expressions but also their perceptual representation, consistent with  predictive  accounts.  Generalization  to  naturalistic  expressions,  other  emotions,and cultures remains to be tested.

articles.title: Common psychiatric treatments alter affective dynamics
articles.authors: Quentin Dercon; Quentin JM Huys; Robb Rutledge; Camilla Nord
articles.abstract: Affective states are dynamic, fluctuating in response to recent events: an unexpected pleasure, a disappointing loss. Affective biases, which cause disruptions in these dynamics, are core components of mental ill-health, but the specific effects of treatments on these biases are poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of common psychiatric treatments on subjective assessments of happiness, confidence, and engagement during a reinforcement learning task (N=935; 130 taking antidepressant medications). Half (N=459) of the participants were randomised to practice a common psychotherapeutic technique—cognitive distancing—throughout the task. From a joint computational model of learning and affect, we find evidence for distinct and overlapping impacts of psychiatric treatments on affective dynamics. Cognitive distancing attenuates downward drift in happiness and engagement and increases recency bias in the affective impact of recent choices. Conversely, antidepressant use increases baseline happiness and confidence in individuals with similar levels of current symptoms, and decreases recency bias such that more past events influence affective states. Crucially, both cognitive distancing and antidepressant use converge to dampen negative biases in happiness and confidence specifically in participants experiencing higher levels of anxiety and depression symptoms. Together, our results indicate that common treatments for mental ill-health may alter symptoms through their impact on affective dynamics, but via distinct mechanisms.

articles.title: A Relevance Rate Model of the affective mechanisms linking social media use to later attentional disruption
articles.authors: Hippolyte Fournier; eva pool; David Sander; Elise Dan-Glauser
articles.abstract: Social media use is increasingly suspected of harming attention, but the evidence remains too limited to draw any firm conclusions. One obstacle is the lack of a framework specifying how such use might affect attention afterwards, without any device. To address this gap, we draw on emotional attention, the affective mechanism that prioritises what matters to individuals. The Relevance Rate Model rests on the relevance rate, the frequency with which an environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli. Drawing on predictive coding, we suggest that social media raises the rate that users expect, and that this expectation may persist after each session and, with repeated use, across daily life. When an activity delivers less concern-relevant information than expected, sustained attention to the ongoing task may be disrupted as emotional attention is recruited to address the shortfall. The model specifies four measurable parameters of use, from which we derive a research agenda.

articles.title: Longitudinal Dataset of Psychological Variables Influencing AI Perception and Usage
articles.authors: Angelica Lermann Henestrosa; Gerrit Anders; Nico Ehrhardt; Anna Christina Faller; Nora Hampel; Irena Vanessa Ivan; Stefanie Helene Klein; Teresa Luther; Mike Prentice; Busra Sarigul
articles.abstract: Since the emergence of large language models (LLMs) in 2022, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly expanded into mainstream applications, leading, for example, to the integration of Apple Intelligence into customer devices in 2024. This integration into personal technology marks a significant shift and a further reduction in barriers to use, bringing advanced AI capabilities into everyday devices and making them accessible to private individuals. Thus, the use of generative AI along with interaction through LLM-powered (voice) assistants and engagement with AI-generated content is expected to increase significantly. However, data that link this usage to psychological variables and shed light on the underlying mechanisms of this use over time remain scarce. In this longitudinal study, data from a US-American sample was collected across six waves at two-month intervals between September 2024 and July 2025. It examines user behavior, attitudes, knowledge, and perceptions related to generative AI. Thus, this dataset allows for future research on psychological and behavioral dynamics of AI usage over time, offering insights into user engagement and the individual factors connected to it.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of self-management on athletic performance: A comment on Fan et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Fan et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking self-management to athletic performance. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Noticing yourself perceiving: Embodied reflexivity, experience design, and evidence at a free arts–science exhibition in India
articles.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Hansika Mangwani; Sanjana Edwankar; Sakina Bharmal; Tanvi Raghuram; Siyona Varghese; Samrddhee Pathare; Amisha Keshan; Ritika Deshpande; Sakshi Kharbanda
articles.abstract: This study evaluates Art of Perception, a seven-zone attraction presented at Creative Lab Festival 2026 in Pune, India. A convergent mixed-methods design combined matched pre-post surveys from 200 visitors (166 complete cases) with learning statements, 1,339 face-judgment votes, and 65 post-workshop drawings. Five of six self-report outcomes showed positive paired differences after Holm correction. Bodily relaxation showed the largest difference (22.9 points on a 0-100 scale; standardised difference = 0.69); trust in perception did not differ reliably. Data indicated learning about perception, neuroplasticity, art-brain relations, and nature connection. The observational, immediate, and self-reported design does not establish causation or durability. The paper proposes a public laboratory of perception as a provisional framework for construct-aligned attraction design and evaluation.

articles.title: From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines? Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI
articles.authors: Olivier LE BON; Xavier Noël
articles.abstract: Randomized trials show that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can reduce conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization. Yet the same systems can increase conspiracy belief when instructed to, and clinical reports describe chatbot conversations accompanying the escalation of implausible convictions. Prevailing accounts attribute both outcomes to the evidence a model supplies. We note that most experiments confound evidence about the world with endorsement of the person, and that the clearest attempt to separate them favors evidence. Drawing on research on attitude certainty, self-validation, and responses to flattery, we distinguish the position of a belief from the certainty with which it is held and formalize γ, an effect of endorsement on certainty at fixed factual content, interpretable as a validation gain. If higher certainty lowers responsiveness to later evidence, the account permits a conditional outcome: beliefs that become less extreme yet more rigid, without any misinformation. We specify two critical experiments, a factorial test of facts and endorsement that includes a source known to approve everyone and an endorsement-first design with counterevidence held constant, plus an articulation control. Conversational AI becomes a test bench for an old question: can social approval make subsequent evidence matter less?

articles.title: People Expect Less but Show Equal Influence of LLM Versus Human Moral Advice
articles.authors: Neele Engelmann; Eva-Madeleine Schmidt; Ali Alhosseini; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Mengchen Dong
articles.abstract: People are often skeptical of AI in the moral domain, yet AI-generated ethical advice can influence moral judgments as much as human advice. Unlike most prior work, which attaches human or AI labels to identical advice, we examined how much real advice written by humans and by AI influences moral judgments, and whether people expect less influence from AI than from human advice. First, we developed 24 realistic everyday moral scenarios and collected over 500 persuasive advice texts from both incentivized human writers (N = 92) and GPT-4o. AI-generated advice was longer, more linguistically complex, more semantically uniform, more virtue-oriented, and less extreme than human advice. Next, a new sample of participants (N = 390) either revised initial moral judgments after receiving human or AI advice or indicated how much they expected such advice to influence them. Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice. Participants who only estimated the influence, however, expected less influence from AI than from human advice. These findings suggest that skepticism toward AI in moral contexts may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.

articles.title: Urban Aesthetics: Beauty and Interestingness of the City
articles.authors: Joerg Fingerhut
articles.abstract:
This paper develops an empirically informed aesthetics of the city by introducing interestingness as a
complementary category to beauty. While beauty has long defined architectural value through
harmony and rightness, urban life also requires experiences of dissonance, openness, and surprise.
Contrasting Scruton’s notion of architectural beauty with Mumford’s conception of the city as secular
and dramatic, I side with Mumford’s more open understanding of urban life.

Conceptually, I propose a middle way that neither centers exclusively on beauty nor simply endorses
a pluralist aesthetics of the city, as is common in contemporary philosophy of the city. To capture the
psychology of urban life, I focus on aesthetic emotions that help explain the experiences of beauty,
interestingness, and belonging. Methodologically, I likewise argue for a middle way that combines
philosophical reflection with empirical research on the psychology and neuroscience of the built
environment. Taken together, the paper outlines an urban-theoretical framework that understands
urban public space, in particular, as an aesthetic interface linking perception, affect, and cognition to
forms of civic participation. Beauty provides coherence; interestingness sustains vitality. Together,
they define the aesthetic and psychological livability of the city.

Keywords
Aesthetic emotions; Affordances; Beauty; Empirical aesthetics; Interestingness; Neurourbanism,
Urban Aesthetics

articles.title: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and spectral features directly drive micro-level autonomic reflexes during brief respiration practices
articles.authors: Jung-tzu Chang; Zai-Fu Yao
articles.abstract:
While digital health platforms increasingly deliver guided mindful breathing interventions via audio, the specific acoustic properties of the guidance are fundamentally ignored as potential active ingredients. This within-subject study implemented an unprecedented high-density experimental design to investigate how distinct, computationally engineered acoustic features (e.g., pitch, zero-crossing rate, natural background sounds) modulate acute cardiovascular, respiratory, and autonomic responses. To rigorously eliminate sex-related physiological variance, 21 meditation-naïve female university students completed 13 randomized audio sessions of a standardized 4-minute-and-5-second guided breathing practice (yielding 273 high-density recording epochs). Multiparametric biosignals, including pulse rate variability (PRV), respiratory dynamics, and electrodermal activity (EDA), were continuously recorded. Results demonstrated a robust reduction in blood pressure independent of audio conditions, confirming the fundamental efficacy of a single bout of spontaneous breath awareness. However, high-resolution analyses revealed a highly modular architecture where peripheral
autonomic indices (EDA and PRV) were acutely sensitive to fine-grained acoustic features, specifically Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs). Furthermore, physiological coupling patterns reorganized dynamically depending strictly on the acoustic context. These indings fundamentally challenge the assumption that meditation audio is a neutral delivery medium, establishing acoustic parameters as potent, independent modulators of human autonomic reflexes for future digital therapeutics.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Contextual modulations at low and high levels of visual perception: functional (in)dependence and influence of local contrast
articles.authors: Mehmet Umut Canoluk; Marius Grandjean; Valerie Goffaux
articles.abstract: What we see depends on context. From low to high levels of the visual system hierarchy, the amplitude of contextual influences is a function of local input strength. In the case of human face perception, the influence exerted by face context on local feature discrimination is determined by that feature discriminability. Face contextual modulations are presumed to rely on high-level, specialized contextual mechanisms, with little contribution of low-level mechanisms. The shared dependence of low- and high-level contextual modulations on local input strength however suggests they may be linked functionally. The present registered report addresses this gap by investigating whether consistent individual differences exist in contextual modulations across low-level contrast detection and high-level facial feature discrimination. Across tasks, we manipulated the contrast (i.e., strength) of a local input target (local grating and eye region, respectively) presented either in isolation or embedded in context. The context in the contrast detection task refers to a larger surrounding grating while it refers to the facial features surrounding the target eye region in the facial feature discrimination task. The comparison of contrast thresholds across conditions provided a metric to evaluate contextual modulation magnitudes. For both upright feature discrimination and contrast detection, context exerted a strong suppressive influence on local target processing; i.e., incongruent face context and parallel surround increased contrast threshold for feature discrimination and grating detection, respectively, compared to isolated viewing condition. As expected, face inversion drastically reduced the influence of context on local contrast threshold. We found no conclusive proof of a functional link between the magnitude of contextual modulation in local contrast detection and face feature matching; there was however extreme evidence for the correlation of contextual modulation magnitude in upright and inverted face feature matching. By investigating the shared variance between the contextual modulation magnitudes across visual processing levels, this study aimed at a system-wide understanding of the influence of spatial context on vision. Despite low- and high-level contextual modulations sharing similar operating principles, the present findings suggest they may involve independent mechanisms. We outline methodological approaches for further research development on this topic.

articles.title: Will members of 12-step recovery groups oppose the use of GLP-1 agonists for addiction?
articles.authors: Wayne Kepner; Steven Klein; Keith Humphreys
articles.abstract: The integration of pharmacotherapy into abstinence-oriented recovery communities has historically been met with friction. However, a new dynamic may be emerging with the rise of GLP-1 agonists (e.g., semaglutide). While robust clinical trial data for GLP-1s regarding the treatment of substance use disorders remains unclear, these new medications are being adopted off-label by innovators in abstinence-oriented treatment facilities and selectively within the 12-step recovery community. This commentary provides an analysis of this phenomenon through the application of Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations theory. We argue that unlike previous medications which faced medication stigma for their psychoactive properties, it may be possible that GLP-1s are being met with less resistance from the recovery community because their mechanism of action is culturally congruent with the 12-step goal of relieving the mental obsession of addiction. We posit that this new phenomenon represents a practice-based evidence signal that deserves attention; perhaps the 12-step recovery community is not as anti-medication as once thought.

articles.title: People Offload Empathy to AI
articles.authors: Madhulika Shastry; Kurt Gray
articles.abstract: Giving empathy is good, but providing emotional support is hard work. Empathic AI gives cheap and easy support, but may be ethically costly. When AI provides empathy, people may feel less compelled to support others. Four studies provide evidence for “empathy offloading:” when people see AI as capable of empathy, they become less willing to empathize with the suffering of others, even without realizing it. When AI seems more capable of empathy people—both with correlations (Study 1) and causal experiments (Study 2)—people report more empathy offloading. When people learn that someone has received emotional support from large language models (LLMs), they engage less with others’ mental states (Study 3) and offer fewer empathic responses (Study 4). Empathic AI might provide low-cost, easily accessible emotional support, but it risks fraying the ethical and emotional commitments we make to other humans. When someone can go cry to AI, why bother getting splashed with their tears?

articles.title: Toward Evidence-Based Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Cross-Domain Systematic Review
articles.authors: Xinyi Wang; Christine Lo; Wei-Hsiang Lo; Manhua Wang; Gaojian Huang
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

articles.title: When an integration composite fails to cohere: host-language orientation as social-world affiliation, and the formative logic behind a failed scale
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Surveys often treat international students' host-language use and "integration" items as measures of one disposition. This article asks what such items measure, and what it means when they fail to cohere. It draws on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study at a national research university in Japan during the shift to online teaching. The data are a survey of international students (N = 176) and 39 interviews with 40 students. Choice of the Japanese survey form was the outcome. Region of origin dominated that choice (Sinosphere odds ratio ≈ 16.2). Three integration indicators were small, could not be separated from origin, and did not cohere (alpha = 0.36). The interviews suggest that the indicators are formative traces of a clustered social world, not reflections of one trait. For such indicators, internal consistency is the wrong test. A low alpha should prompt the question of what the items jointly index.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-informed Psychoeducation for Eating Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Olivia Chapman; Kira Venables; Abigail Smith; Amanda Makara; Kevin Danaher; Sarah Daniels; Falzah Farooq; Ann Frances Haynos
articles_hidden.abstract: Eating disorders are serious psychological concerns associated with high levels of physical and psychological comorbidity and elevated premature mortality rates. Despite the severity of these disorders, gaps in clinical care exist and most individuals with eating disorders either do not receive or do not benefit from existing evidence-based treatments. There has been a growing movement to incorporate neuroscience-informed targets into eating disorder treatment; however, to date psychoeducation for eating disorders remains narrowly focused on eating- and weight-related behaviors and less directed towards their underlying mechanisms. Yet, neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) can provide vital insights into diagnostic distinctions, patterns of psychiatric comorbidity, risk and maintenance mechanisms, brain-body relations, prognostic course, and therapeutic targets for eating disorders. Further, knowledge of neuroscience can assist in designing the delivery of psychoeducation with the neurobiology of eating disorders in mind by tailoring content to consider the impact of personality and illness stage on the learning process. In this chapter, we highlight the promise of NIPE for eating disorders, provide a case example of NIPE for eating disorders delivered in a clinical setting, and discuss future directions for research in this area. Ultimately, NIPE can be used to bridge the gap between research knowledge and clinical care in eating disorders, thereby enhancing patient self-efficacy, dispelling misconceptions about eating disorders, and enhancing the accessibility of the science for individuals with these serious, yet undertreated disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Accelerometer-Measured Activity and Psychological Well-Being in Older Adults: A Multilevel Longitudinal Analysis of NHATS Data
articles_hidden.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: To examine whether objectively measured activity was associated with psychological well-being in older adults and whether social participation and digital connectivity were related to these associations.
Methods: Using three waves of accelerometer and survey data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (2022–2024), this analysis applied multilevel models with within-between decomposition to examine three activity indicators (mean activity, relative amplitude, and behavioral fragmentation) and four well-being outcomes (loneliness, positive affect, meaning and purpose, and self-determination) in 543 participants. Between-person structural equation models examined social participation as a statistical correlate, and cross-level interactions tested digital connectivity as a moderator of within-person associations.
Results: At the between-person level, fragmentation was associated with three of four outcomes (positive affect, meaning and purpose, self-determination), whereas mean activity was associated with one (positive affect); seven of 24 coefficients survived Bonferroni correction. Mean activity showed within-person associations with loneliness and positive affect. Relative amplitude showed no association surviving correction. Exploratory indirect associations through social participation were significant for positive affect, meaning and purpose, and self-determination, but not loneliness. None of the 12 cross-level interactions was significant (all ps ≥ .069).
Discussion: Older adults with less fragmented daily activity, characterized by fewer shifts from active to sedentary states, reported higher well-being than their peers. In years when participants were more active than their own usual level, they reported less loneliness and more positive affect. Social participation statistically accounted for part of the between-person associations. These findings are observational and based on a selected subsample.

articles_hidden.title: Development and validation of a task for assessing help-seeker relational dynamics.
articles_hidden.authors: Tyler Kwan; Jae Shin; Caroline Selai; Orestis Zavlis; Michael Moutoussis
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers. However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity. Quantitative analyses can validate the task’s measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation. In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the “Helping Task” based on the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized help-provider, in which both parties invested effort (points). Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 ‘neurotypical’, 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation). Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships. Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task’s sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort. Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship. These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.

articles_hidden.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist
articles_hidden.authors: Sacha Epskamp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies. I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow. The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them. AI is now the better jack of all trades. When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible. I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological education
so that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them. The
specialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, while
quantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: How Feminine and Masculine Do Cisgender People in the U.S. Think the Average Gender Nonbinary Person Is?
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Reiman
articles_hidden.abstract: Perception of gender is ubiquitous and consequential in social life. People who are perceived as women are expected to enact femininity, whereas people who are perceived as men are expected to enact masculinity. How do gender nonbinary people fit into these binary assumptions? The present work examined the perceived femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people. In particular, cisgender primarily straight/heterosexual U.S.-based participants reported their assumptions about the assigned sex (Study 1; N = 315) or their perceptions of the femininity and masculinity (Studies 2-3; Ns = 216 and 277) of the average nonbinary person. No apparent bias in terms of assumed sex or perceived femininity emerged, yet participants rated the average nonbinary person as reliably below the scale midpoint on masculinity. Accordingly, straight cisgender Americans’ perceptions of the average nonbinary person may in part reflect a tendency to safeguard masculinity.

articles_hidden.title: The Map Is Not the Territory: Construct Names, Items, and Responses in Measures of Mentalizing, Epistemic Trust, and Emotion Regulation
articles_hidden.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Marco Marelli; Laura Antonia Lucia Parolin; Karin Ensink
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. This matters most for constructs theorized as interdependent. In theory, these constructs are defined by name, and their interdependence is posited at that level; in practice, each is measured by a pool of items, often from separate questionnaires, which may overlap or diverge in ways the names do not anticipate. We asked whether construct names correspond to the items that operationalize them, whether items reflect the structure of responses, and whether responses follow the boundaries posited by names or drawn by items. Using reflective functioning, epistemic trust, and difficulties in emotion regulation as a case study, we compared semantic similarities of construct names and items with response correlations in 1,167 emerging adults (aged 18–29, 72% female; item-level analyses preregistered) and 1,068 secondary school students (aged 14–20, 67% female). Construct names best matched their own items in 4 of 11 subscales. Items reflected the structure of responses (r = .62 and .58), also, less closely, across questionnaires (.42 and .37). Responses followed boundaries drawn by items more than those posited by names. A correlation between such measures, usually read as evidence of interdependence, may also arise from items that describe the same experience or from shared method variance. What theory says about a construct thus applies only in part to what its items measure.

articles_hidden.title: Fast or Slow? Individual and Symptom Differences in the Dynamic Speed of Psychopathological Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Liying Zhang; Xinchun Wu; Luming Liu; Ying Li; Wenchao Wang; Hao Yuan; Yang Li; Jingmeng Cui
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Recent research has increasingly adopted complex dynamical systems theory to understand psychopathology. A key proposition is that psychopathological symptoms may operate at different time scales, with different dynamic speeds shaping the evolution of the symptom system. This study examined the extent to which variability in symptom dynamic speed reflects symptom differences, person differences, and person-by-symptom interactions.
Methods: We analyzed five intensive longitudinal experience sampling datasets comprising 265 participants and 33,059 retained observations. Dynamic speed was quantified for each person-symptom time series using lag-1 autocorrelation (AC) and mean period (MP) derived from Lomb–Scargle spectral analysis. Multilevel variance decomposition was used to partition variability into person, symptom, and person-by-symptom components.
Results: Across the two dynamic speed indices, symptom variance was generally non-significant. Person variance and person-by-symptom interaction variance were significant in several datasets and generally exceeded symptom variance, although pairwise differences between variance components were not consistently significant.
Conclusion: The findings provide limited evidence for consistent symptom differences in dynamic speed; person differences and person-by-symptom interactions may play a more prominent role. These results highlight the importance of idiographic approaches to understanding symptom dynamics and underscore the need for further research into the clinical implications of dynamic speed.

articles_hidden.title: Specifying Innateness in Infant Development: A Framework for Theory-Building Based on Co-Determination
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Infant research has often treated early neural and behavioral expression as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, with early-emerging capacities sometimes uncritically taken as evidence of innate knowledge. This paper evaluates the strength of such inferences through four intersecting lenses: genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, definitional precision, and standards of scientific explanation and falsifiability. It distinguishes among several non-equivalent forms of innateness, including claims about representational content, architectural or processing biases, developmental canalization, and maturational timing. In place of broad or underspecified appeals to innateness, it advances co-determination as a framework for theory-building that encourages specification of the biological constraints, experiential inputs, cultural ecologies, developmental timing, and interactive mechanisms proposed to produce a given outcome, as well as the patterns of variation that would support or challenge those claims. The central aim is to provide a more precise and testable basis for theorizing about the initial state of the infant mind.

articles_hidden.title: Brain synchrony between interacting sibling pairs during real-time cooperation: an fMRI hyperscanning study
articles_hidden.authors: Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Arezoo Taebi; Julia Koch; Klaus Mathiak; Lisa Wagels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships. Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions. Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings. In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination. Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas. 

The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05). These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus). Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration. Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05). 

This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks. We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological preparation in multimodal cancer prehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-synthesis of patients’ experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Baliousis; Aniqa Hussain; Zachary Underwood; Thomas Albert Schroder; Mike Rennoldson; Chloe Grimmett; Hermioni L. Amonoo; Sandy Jack
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Prehabilitation aims to optimise psychological status, but psychological provision largely addresses existing distress and what preparation for treatment consists of is unclear as prehabilitation services scale up. We asked how patients experience it, what enables or undermines it, and how their circumstances shape what they can use.

Methods: We searched CINAHL, MEDLINE and PsycINFO from inception, last searched 22 May 2026, for peer-reviewed English-language qualitative studies of adults’ experiences of multimodal cancer prehabilitation. Eligible programmes combined at least two of exercise, nutrition and psychological support, and either targeted psychological outcomes or included an element with a stated psychological function; measurement alone did not qualify. Two reviewers appraised reports using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist plus four domains covering staff training, fidelity, adherence and participants’ words. We synthesised findings by meta-ethnography. No external funding. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123).

Results: Seventeen reports (2021-2026), predominantly surgical and from six high-income countries, drew on 14 independent samples and 230 patients. Across three constructs and 12 subthemes, patients experienced psychological preparation as having something to act on, discovering what their bodies could do, understanding and managing what was coming, being taken seriously and kept going, and not being alone. These functions arose through exercise, dietary support and relationships with staff and peers, not only explicitly psychological input. Prehabilitation added to preparations already under way. Relevance, timing, burden and continuity after surgery enabled or undermined preparation, depending on patients’ beliefs, capacity, demands and support networks.

Discussion: Evidence came almost entirely from engagers, and staff training, adherence and fidelity were sparsely reported. Psychological preparation did not map onto a discrete component; it arose where what a programme offered matched what a patient could use. Services should build psychological function into how prehabilitation is delivered, who delivers it, and how it is matched to patients.

articles_hidden.title: MASEMiner – AI-Assisted Data Extraction  for Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Timo Gnambs; Johanna Einsiedler
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) synthesizes multivariate evidence across studies, allowing researchers to examine theory-driven path models, including mediated and predictive effects, and to evaluate the dimensional structure of psychological and behavioral measures. A major bottleneck is the labor-intensive extraction of statistical information from primary studies. Large language models and vision-language models offer new opportunities for extracting such heterogeneous statistics from textual and visual document content. Building on these capabilities, we introduce MASEMiner, an open-source application for AI-assisted extraction and verification of data required for MASEM that can be run locally or accessed through a hosted web interface. MASEMiner supports the extraction of directly reported correlations and related effect sizes as well as indirect information (i.e., factor loadings and factor correlations) used to reconstruct correlation matrices for MASEM. We evaluated MASEMiner in four use cases against human-coded reference databases from published meta-analyses, using separate study sets for prompt development and evaluation. Factor loadings were extracted with near-perfect accuracy (sensitivity ≥ 0.92, precision ≥ 0.98), whereas directly reported effect sizes were recovered completely (sensitivity = 1.00) but with lower precision (0.54–0.69) due to overextraction. In a verification study with four coders, automated extraction plus human verification reduced coding time on average by 42% relative to manual extraction at comparable accuracy. MASEMiner thus supports a human-in-the-loop workflow that reduces manual coding effort while preserving transparency and reproducibility in research synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: A Multi-Regional Study Comparing Perceived Risks between Face-to-Face versus Digital Mental Health Services - Associations with Differences in Preferences and Behavioral Intentions and the Moderation of Self-Construal: A Cross-Sectional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Siu Kit Yeung; Winnie W. S. Mak; Ben C. L. Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Recent studies have investigated preferences and perceptions towards face-to-face and digital psychological interventions. Understanding the potential differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital services as well as associations with preferences and intentions, can be worthwhile.
Objectives:
We investigated differences in perceived likelihood of being found out and perceived severity of face loss between face-to-face psychological interventions and digital psychological interventions. We also tested the associations between differences in perceived risks and differences in intentions or preferences towards different types of interventions, and investigated the potential moderation of self-construal, regulatory focus, and cultural background. 
Methods:
We conducted a multi-regional study with 645 college students in Hong Kong China, India, United Kingdom, and Canada. We performed t-tests, correlation analyses, and moderated multiple regressions, while combining with alternative statistical methods to examine robustness and consistency of findings across methods.
Results:
We found that people generally perceive face-to-face interventions to have higher likelihood of being found out and severity of face loss compared to digital interventions, with medium to large effects. While no significant association was found for the difference in perceived likelihood of being found out with the difference in intervention preferences and help-seeking intentions, higher perceived severity of face loss for face-to-face intervention was associated with lower preferences and intentions for face-to-face intervention relative to digital interventions. Such associations are moderated by self-construal but in the opposite direction to our hypotheses, in which people with stronger independent self-construal had stronger negative associations between difference in perceived severity of face loss and difference in preferences or intentions. 
Conclusions:
Our findings contribute by identifying differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital interventions as well as association with preferences and intentions. We speculate the surprising self-construal moderation findings may be due to higher reliance on personal feelings and higher prioritization for self-consistency among more independent people, and call for further studies testing such mechanisms. We encourage further much-needed investigations into various forms of perceived risks and potential associations with face-to-face or digital mental health intervention preferences, intentions, and decisions, while examining individual and cultural factors.

Keywords: Digital Psychological Interventions, Face-to-Face Psychological Interventions, Help-Seeking, Risk Perception, Face Loss, Self-Construal

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles_hidden.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-reasoning, the ability to monitor progress and regulate effort during reasoning, comprises monitoring and control. Monitoring, including confidence, is assumed to guide control processes. Yet, whether monitoring and control compete with reasoning for shared cognitive resources is unclear. To address this, we examined the role of working memory in reasoning and meta-reasoning, drawing on Fuzzy Trace Theory and the meta-reasoning framework. Participants (N = 998) solved syllogisms with and without validity-believability conflict in a two-response paradigm under six constraint conditions. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined. Confidence was lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems and reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time across all conditions. Monitoring resolution, however, was low throughout. These results suggest cognitive constraints impair reasoning generally but largely spare conflict-detection and control sensitivity. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a general monitoring limitations rather than constrained resources.

articles_hidden.title: Avoiding Feelings and Resisting Closeness: A Network Analysis of Attachment and Affect Regulation in Adolescents with Mental Health Concerns
articles_hidden.authors: Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents with mental health concerns often experience difficulties navigating attachment relationships and regulating emotions. Although attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties are well-established transdiagnostic risk factors for adolescent psychopathology, far less is known about the specific experiences and beliefs that connect these domains. Understanding these connections may provide insight into how attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties mutually reinforce one another. The present study used a cross-sectional network analysis to examine item-level associations among attachment and affect regulation in a clinical sample of 608 adolescents (57% female; Mage = 13.98, SD = 2.36) referred to publicly funded youth mental health services. Community detection analyses identified four interconnected dimensions corresponding to attachment anxiety, attachment avoidance, affect dysregulation/suppression, and affect reflection. Notably, affect dysregulation and suppression formed a unified community when examined alongside attachment, suggesting that emotional overwhelm and emotional avoidance may function as closely interconnected aspects of emotional functioning. Two bridge nodes emerged as key points of connection between attachment and affect regulation: the belief that “thinking about my feelings just makes everything worse” and the experience of wanting closeness with a parent while simultaneously pulling away. These findings highlight beliefs about emotions and uncertainty regarding interpersonal closeness and support as important points of connection between attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties. Implications for attachment-informed intervention and future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Physiological Hyperarousal in the Relationship Between Insomnia and Nightmare Proneness
articles_hidden.authors: William E. Kelly; Ani Enriquez; Faith Yanez
articles_hidden.abstract: Nightmare proneness has been associated with insomnia beyond nightmare frequency and neuroticism. The present study examined physiological hyperarousal as a potential process contributing to this relationship. Participants were 209 adults recruited from a university participant pool and an online community sample. Participants completed self-report measures of nightmare proneness, insomnia, physiological hyperarousal, nightmare frequency, neuroticism, and trauma symptoms. Hierarchical regression and indirect-effect analyses were conducted. After controlling for recruitment source, age, gender, nightmare frequency, neuroticism, and trauma symptoms, nightmare proneness explained an additional 6.5% of the variance in insomnia. Physiological hyperarousal accounted for an additional 2.3% of variance beyond nightmare proneness. Nightmare proneness showed a significant indirect association with insomnia through physiological hyperarousal but maintained a direct association with insomnia after physiological hyperarousal was considered. Physiological hyperarousal may represent one process contributing to the relationship between nightmare proneness and insomnia but does not fully account for this association. The findings support conceptualizing nightmare proneness and physiological hyperarousal as related but non-redundant factors associated with insomnia.

articles_hidden.title: Age-Related Neural Dedifferentiation Is Driven by Declining Reliability
articles_hidden.authors: Tiantian Yang; Molly Simmonite; Ethan Maddox; Bingjie Liu; Thad Polk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Neural dedifferentiation, characterized by reduced distinctiveness of neural representations, is a robust feature of cognitive aging. Multivoxel pattern analyses often operationalize neural distinctiveness as the difference between within-category similarity (reliability) and between-category similarity (confusability). However, it remains unclear whether age-related reductions in distinctiveness are driven by decreases in reliability, increases in confusability, or both, and whether these components demonstrate similar longitudinal trajectories. Using cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) study, we decomposed distinctiveness into its two components across visual, auditory, and motor cortex in more than 200 young (18-29 years) and older adults (65-94 years) and estimated cross-sectional between-person age differences and longitudinal within-person change simultaneously in mixed-effects models. We found that reliability was lower in older vs. younger adults cross-sectionally, and this reduction was significantly larger than the corresponding effect on confusability. Moreover, reliability also declined longitudinally within individuals across a mean interval of four years. These findings indicate that age-related dedifferentiation is driven primarily by declining reliability rather than increasing confusability, and that reporting distinctiveness alone can conceal substantial age-related change in its components. 
Keywords: Dedifferentiation, distinctiveness, reliability, confusability, aging, longitudinal study

articles_hidden.title: Infants’ Social Evaluations Revisited: An Updated Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Margoni; Alvin Wei Ming Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past twenty years, numerous studies have suggested that infants prefer prosocial agents—who help, comfort, or act fairly—over antisocial agents, who harm others or act unfairly. However, the field has faced replication challenges, including a recent multi-lab failed replication, raising concerns about the robustness of these effects. In response, we updated and extended an earlier meta-analysis, synthesizing 182 effect sizes from published and unpublished studies, with an aggregate sample of 4,089 infants aged 0–32 months, using manual choice and visual preference measures. The estimated meta-analytic raw proportion for infants’ preference for prosocial over antisocial agents was 0.65, 95% CI [0.61, 0.68]. This preference was largely stable across age, type of measure, stimulus format, and scenario type, but there was some evidence that larger studies yielded smaller effects. No clear evidence of publication bias was detected.

articles_hidden.title: Saccade Selection Predictably Changes With Load
articles_hidden.authors: Zakaria Gefferie; Estelle Coelingh; Christoph Strauch
articles_hidden.abstract: Departing from traditional information-maximization accounts, recent work proposes that saccade selection arbitrates economically between the expected benefits and costs of shifting attention. We tested this economic account by manipulating the cognitive resources available during selection, arguing that reduced resources should increase the weight of costs, thereby altering selection. Across two experiments, participants selected between saccade targets while performing a non-spatial memory task that manipulated cognitive load. Targets appeared in directions with previously and independently established intrinsic (effort) costs, quantified through pupillometry. In Experiment 1, monetary rewards were staircased against participants' choices, replicating that money can compensate for intrinsic costs. This yielded an informative reward range from which Experiment 2 sampled randomly. Experiment 2 revealed that higher memory load biased selection toward cost-efficient saccades, while reward sensitivity remained unaffected.Load also selectively shortened the long latency tail, consistent with reduced deliberation under increased load and therefore an increased weight on deliberation cost. Saccade selection thus depends on available cognitive resources, supporting an economic account of visual selection over information maximization accounts.

articles_hidden.title: Music therapists’ attitudes, motivation, and use of treatment manuals: a survey study
articles_hidden.authors: Theo Dimitriadis; Wendy L. Magee; Andrea W.M. Evers; Rebecca S Schaefer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction
Treatment manuals and protocols (TM/Ps) are increasingly used to standardise clinical interventions in music therapy, but they often neglect the motivational needs of clients, which are essential for engagement and recovery. Therapists may, at times, modify or depart from established protocols in order to accommodate clients’ interests, preferences, or motivational needs. This study had two aims: to examine music therapists’ attitudes, practices, and reasons for deviation regarding TM/P use, and to introduce a novel, motivation-driven TM/P targeting a client group where motivation is crucial: clients in the subacute phase after stroke. 

Method
Qualified music therapists (N=93) from five countries completed an online survey addressing demographic background, theoretical orientation, opinions, and behaviour surrounding protocol use, and reasons for deviation. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise the sample; hypotheses were tested using crosstabulations with χ² tests of independence and ordinal logistic regression analysis. 

Results
Music therapists held mixed views on TM/Ps, recognising their value while expressing concerns about impacts on personalisation, spontaneity, and motivation. Many agreed that non-client-focused protocols negatively affect motivation and identified spontaneity restrictions as problematic, though these concerns did not significantly predict actual usage patterns. Usage varied partially by setting (lower in educational contexts), theoretical approach (lower in anthroposophic and attachment-oriented and higher in integrative approaches), and specific attitudes toward TM/P importance, rather than by therapist experience or age, suggesting that contextual factors and individual beliefs about protocol value outweigh demographic characteristics in determining TM/P usage. 

Discussion
Findings highlight the ongoing tension between standardisation and personalisation in music therapy, reflecting shared practitioner concerns. Building on these insights and prior applications, the ReMoCo-IMS Protocol, a motivation-driven TM/P for subacute stroke rehabilitation, is introduced. This protocol advances flexible, evidence-based guidelines that support both clinical rigour and motivational, client-centred care.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational Sex Segregation is Strongly Predicted by Psychological Sex Differences
articles_hidden.authors: Joakim Karl Erik Frostegård; Björn Persson; Kimmo Sorjonen; Kåre Hedebrant; Mikael Lundqvist; Agneta Herlitz
articles_hidden.abstract: If traits of individuals are associated with occupational choice, sex differences in those traits should be associated with sex differences in occupational choice, and consequently, with occupational sex segregation. In this cross-sectional study, we assessed the extent to which this is the case for spatial ability, verbal ability, agreeableness, emotional stability, interest in people and interest in things, across 429 occupations. Participants (N = 2,576, aged 35-45) completed online tests and questionnaires, while students rated occupational requirements. For each occupation, the population sex composition of people with traits in line with requirements was estimated, using trait sex differences and occupational requirement profiles. Estimates were highly predictive of actual population sex ratios, with the model assessing interest and cognition in conjunction explaining the most variance (R2 = .49), followed by the interest model (R2 = .46) and the cognition model (R2 = .18). Among individual traits, sex differences in interest in things were by far the most predictive (R2 = .42). Notably, sex differences in cognition were more predictive of high proportions of men in occupations than high proportions of women. Given lifespan trait stability, these results suggest that cognition and interests matter in occupational choice, with sex differences consequently contributing substantially to occupational sex segregation.

articles_hidden.title: Challenging “nature” as a causal category: An environmental bundle approach to restorative experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Yannick Joye; Andreas de Block; Dylan Chau Huynh
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on restorative environments has long examined the psychological benefits of contact with nature. Findings from this work are often interpreted as showing that nature itself causes restoration. In this article, we provide both a critical assessment of this causal claim, and propose an alternative “bundle” approach. In the first part, we assess whether nature satisfies two requirements for a scientifically useful causal category: coherence and mechanistic relevance.
